name: Note
text: Before touching anything: check plate resolution, frame rate, and color space (log vs. Rec.709). Note lens info if given (focal length, distortion). A shaky handheld plate needs stabilizing BEFORE roto or tracking, not after — everything downstream inherits plate motion.

name: Note
text: Roto the subject on 1s first for fast motion, every 3-5 frames for slow motion, then fill gaps. Use Bezier for hard edges, B-spline/roto brush for hair/fur/motion blur edges. Feather 1-2px minimum — a razor-sharp roto edge is the #1 beginner tell.

name: Note
text: Planar track for flat surfaces (screens, signs, walls). Point track + camera solve for 3D insert work. Always verify the track by parenting a test null/checker pattern to it and scrubbing the WHOLE shot, not just a few frames.

name: Note
text: Sample the key color from a flat, evenly-lit patch, never a shadowed corner. Check the alpha channel alone (not just the composite) for holes and noise before moving on. Spill-suppress after keying, not before — order matters.

name: Note
text:
1. Roto/key
2. Color-match CG or foreground to plate (black levels, white balance, grain)
3. Add light wrap where elements meet
4. Match motion blur and depth of field
5. Grain/noise pass last, applied to the WHOLE comp so it reads as one image

name: Note
text:
1. Mismatched black levels between plate and added element
2. No motion blur on a fast-moving comped object
3. Hard, unfeathered keying/roto edges
4. Grain only on the plate, not on what you added
5. Perfectly clean added element next to a noisy/grainy real plate

name: Note
text: DaVinci Resolve Fusion — free, node-based, a genuinely good first real compositor. Blender — free, also handles 3D if you want to add CG elements later. Note here which one you're using and why, so tutorials/settings stay consistent.

name: Note
text: A "floating object" shot (rig/wire removal + a believable idle motion). A day-to-night sky replacement with matching color temp shift on the foreground. A simple muzzle-flash or energy-beam effect added to a phone-shot video, with correct light interaction on nearby surfaces.

name: Note
text: Drop the actual shot plates here (image or video cards), plus any on-set reference photos and lens-grid/gray-ball/chrome-ball shots if you have them. Everything in the sections to the left refers back to whatever lands in this column.
